paper_title: More Memory, Better Videos? A Controlled Study of Visual Memory in Long-Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-video generators increasingly retrieve past visual observations to prevent identity drift. The intuition is compelling: more access to history should make future video more consistent. But an image can be faithful to the past and wrong for the present. Does visual memory always improve the generated story? We investigate this question through VMem-Bench, a two-track diagnostic study. Track-A measures which references are selected from 92 real films (16,548 segments), before generation and without generator confounds. Track-B compares four retrieval policies with no-memory and gold-informed last-seen controls on 30 causally generated stories (2,824 segments) using a shared generator. Retrieval increases entity recall from 0.559 to 0.628-0.693 and improves similarity to past appearances, but decreases precision from 0.977 to 0.915-0.938 and forbidden-entity avoidance from 0.968 to 0.845-0.898. It can also reinforce obsolete appearances after the story changes them. Conversely, high long-gap recall can arise without memory when the prompt itself supplies the appearance; an appearance-stripping analysis exposes this confound. These results distinguish historical fidelity from current-story correctness and show why retrieval relevance or final-video consistency alone does not establish memory utility.

Dataset: huggingface.co/datasets/Suchenl/VMem-Bench Code: github.com/Suchenl/VMem-Bench Project Page: suchenl.github.io/VMem-Bench 1 1. Introduction More memory, better videos? Causal long-video generation produces sequence of segments while carrying past observations forward [11, 21, 24]. Historical retrieval can restore visual context when character returns [4, 23]. Other systems compress frame or KV histories [7, 26], or organize memory by entity [2, 8]. Memory-conditioned storytelling likewise uses earlier shots to anchor later appearances [17, 25]. But the story may have changed: the character wears new outfit, an object has been destroyed, or deceased person is mentioned without being present. retrieved frame can improve fidelity to history while making the current segment less correct  (Fig. 1)  . Beyond perceptual and cross-shot consistency measured by existing evaluations [3, 6, 20]: when does access to visual history actually help generation, and when does it introduce interference? Three confounds complicate this question. First, the current prompt may already describe returning entity. Second, historical matching may preserve obsolete appearances; state tracking differs from identity anchoring [8, 29]. Third, relevant references may contain now-forbidden entities. Retrieval evaluation separates relevance, downstream utility, and distracting evidence [14]. For visual generation, current-state correctness and entity exclusion must be measured alongside historical resemblance. We use VMem-Bench to separate what memory retrieves from what the generator does with it. At step n, policy reads references (cid:98)Cn from historical memory Mn for instruction gn; the generator then produces xn: Mn R(gn) (cid:98)Cn G(gn) xn. (1) Track-A replays 92 real films, evaluating reference selection against frozen entity-level gold before the next segment is revealed. Track-B runs 30 authored stories causally, comparing four retrieval policies with no-memory and goldinformed last-seen controls under one video-generation pipeline. These matched-prompt comparisons evaluate complete policies: each policy writes its own history. They are not single-step interventions, and the two tracks use different instances. An unexpected answer. Within this controlled setting, retrieval improves overall entity recall and appearance similarity to historical renderings. Yet it also decreases precision and forbidden-entity avoidance; on changed-state returns it can restore an outdated appearance. Long-gap success partly reflects prompt information: no-memory generation can achieve high recall when instructions describe the entity. Memory utility therefore requires checking what history adds, which temporal state is valid, and what unwanted content it brings. These findings concern visual-history utility, not memory-capacity scaling law. Contributions. controlled characterization of memorys trade-offs. We show, across four retrieval policies and two controls, that historical references increase recall and appearance continuity while also increasing unwanted appearances and sometimes conflicting with updated story states. Evidence of an evaluation confound. targeted appearance-stripping analysis shows why successful longgap reappearance can reflect prompt information rather than long-range memory. We separate historical appearance similarity, present-state correctness, and entity exclusion. reusable diagnostic study framework. VMem-Bench combines pre-generation evidence analysis (92 films, 16,548 segments, 2,803 entities) and post-generation, closed-loop evaluation (30 stories, 2,824 segments, nine memory stresses), with controlled retrieval comparisons, frozen scoring, and explicit limitations on attribution. 2. Related Work Visual memory for video generation. Visual histories support causal generation through compressed frame or KV context [7, 22, 26], historical retrieval [4, 23, 28], and entity-indexed state [2, 8, 29]. OneStory learns adaptive historical-frame conditioning [1]; StoryMem learns memoryconditioned multi-shot generation [25]. LiveEdit studies streaming editing with content-preservation constraints [18]; broader survey organizes controllable video conditioning mechanisms [9]. Holding the generator fixed across retrieval policies, we test whether reference relevance and historical resemblance predict current-story correctness. Long-video and memory benchmarks. VBench measures perceptual and semantic quality [6]. MovieBench, MSVBench, and EntityBench evaluate movie-level or crossshot consistency [3, 15, 20]; MBench and NarraStreamBench test memory or narrative consistency [8, 27]. SubjectAnchor combines subject-aware memory with trained video model and its own storytelling benchmark, including shot-level inclusion/exclusion control [17]. Our two tracks measure selected evidence before generation and story correctness afterward, complementing these evaluations and SubjectAnchors inclusion/exclusion tests. This does not establish superiority over its trained architecture (Supplementary Table 12; App. C). Retrieval relevance and downstream utility. LongMemEval and MemoryAgentBench connect memory operations to task success [5, 19]. RAGChecker already separates retrieval quality from generation quality and identifies distracting evidence [14]. Our question concerns temporal 2 validity in visual generation: historical appearance continuity can coexist with an incorrect current state or an unwanted entity. We jointly test selected evidence, updated states, forbidden appearances, and prompt-information sensitivity. No-memory controls check what history adds beyond the current instruction, while complete-policy comparisons measure the outcome of each evolving memory history, with explicit limits on causal attribution. screen. Track-B measures what survives generation, with shared pipeline across conditions (Sec. 4.1). Because each condition updates memory from its own output, their histories diverge during the closed-loop rollout. Scoring gold describes entities and states; it is hidden from ordinary policies and used only for scoring, except for the explicitly privileged gold-ID Last-seen diagnostic (App. C.4). It supplies no reference pixels or descriptions. 3. Study Design: Evidence and Outcomes 3.2. Data, Gold, and Memory Stresses To study the utility of history, we observe two points in Eq. 1: the references policy selects before generation (Track-A) and the video produced afterward (Track-B). VMem-Bench is the experimental instrument for this investigation; Fig. 2a shows the two protocols. For example, Track-A asks whether selected references cover puppy requested in later segment of the real film Spring  (Fig. 12)  . Track-B instead tests memory use in independently authored, generated stories, with no-memory and last-seen controls. The two tracks measure complementary boundaries, not matched instances. 3.1. This check does not rule out systematic judging errors or bias from nonrandom missingness. Crop-conditioned H3 changes the input pathway too; its copying failures are analyzed separately in App. F.6. 5. Conclusion More memory does not necessarily mean better videos. In our controlled study, retrieved history improves entity recall and resemblance to earlier appearances, yet can reintroduce retired entities and reinforce obsolete states. Detailed prompts can also make long-gap generation succeed without visual memory. The practical lesson is to assess three distinct questions: what information history adds, which temporal state is valid, and what unwanted content accompanies useful evidence. Report these alongside perceptual quality; recall or historical resemblance alone does not establish memory utility. VMem-Bench provides evidenceand generation-stage measurements, with an evaluation checklist in App. A. These are assessment principles, not validated controller or universal memory-capacity law.

Data and cohort coverage: App. B; systems, controls, and reproduction: App. C; scoring and calibration: App. D; additional Track-A and Track-B results: Apps. and F; author audit: App. G; design implications and limitations: App. H. A. Evaluation Lessons and Reader Checklist What to take away. The study identifies three questions that memory evaluation should keep distinct: whether history supplies information beyond the current instruction and any baseline context, whether its appearance matches the requested temporal state, and whether useful references carry unwanted entities. These are measurement questions, not sufficient decision rule for reading memory. For example, prompt describing blue coat may still omit the face; textual detail alone does not establish that visual history is redundant. Likewise, an older appearance can be correct for an explicit flashback: validity is relative to the instruction, not simply reference recency. Table 10 turns the findings into reporting actions. Figure 8. From S1 draft to frozen gold. In two Spring segments, the VLM draft describes the action but leaves entities that are on screen unnamed, and the first draft also borrows an action from the next segment. The frozen instruction names every present entity by its roster name, so memory can be asked for each of them. The footer counts the same kind of change over the whole corpus. own generated history. Track-A scores refer to selected reference items and entity coverage; Track-B scores refer to rendered appearances. The original tracks use different stories, so neither their absolute scores nor story-level associations form paired retrieval-to-generation analysis. To study that relationship, use matched inputs and retain both reference and output measurements. Read outcomes before rankings. description-matching presence hit need not establish the same individual; high similarity to the previous appearance need not establish the correct current state. Similarity conditions on detection in both appearances, so inspect visibility and missing returns before treating it as an unconditional success rate. In the sharedgenerator block, compare each policy with no memory using the recall/precision/Avoid-OK vector. Higher values are better for those three rates, but higher old-appearance similarity is ambiguous after requested state change. Nativegenerator rows compare whole systems; Last-seen is privileged, variable-budget diagnostic control. Neither supplies memory-only ranking against the shared-generator retrieval policies. Choose the measurement boundary first. Decisions to read, filter, or reject history remain hypotheses in Table 25; evidence for measurement problem alone does not validate its proposed remedy. B. Data Construction and Cohort Coverage B.1. Benchmark Construction Pipeline (S1S4) Track-A gold is built in four stages followed by deterministic freeze. Model outputs are replaceable proposals; stable identifiers, prompt completeness, and frozen gold are fixed by deterministic contracts and human adjudication. S1 drafts bounded segments, present entities, first appearances, and finite-ontology state events; human-confirmed canonical roster is the naming authority. S2 deterministically normalizes schema, identifiers, timestamps, and duplicates and runs structural linting. S3 reviews each segment with Qwen3-VL-8B [13]; low-confidence/conflicting presence claims are rechecked and confirmed entities trigger deterministic prompt repair. Each unit receives PASS, WARN, BLOCK, or RETRYABLEERROR. S4 sends every BLOCK plus stratified audit sample of the remaining units to blocking human review. Accepted decisions re-run the full deterministic validator. The final freeze writes the gold registry and layout hash; changed layout/exclusion set creates new data version. Every stage writes derived artifact and never mutates the original draft. Fig. 7 summarizes both tracks construction, and Fig. 8 shows what the Track-A stages change in practice. B.2. Anatomy of Frozen Gold Instance frozen Track-A movie is an ordered sequence of promptcomplete intents with harness-side typed entity records, lifecycle/state events, required memory records, and forbidden/deprecated records. Only the current intent and, after reveal, the real segment are visible to the system. Typed gold identities, persistent gold records, required targets, and forbidden targets remain scoring-only. Entity records use {character, prop, location} with canonical names and aliases. Track-As reappearance, multi-instance, scenereturn, and state-change labels are diagnostic tags over this same frozen structure. Fig. 9 shows one frozen film. B.3. Authored Stories and Cohort Coverage Track-B story is authored rather than annotated: human writes the entities, their states, look-alike pairs, and scenes, and the scoring gold and prompt stream are derived from that skeleton. Fig. 10 shows how one story places every memory stress on its timeline. Coverage of the evaluated stories. Table 11 summarizes only the 30 evaluated stories, not the larger authoring pool. They contain 2,824 segments, with median 87.5 and range 68131 segments, and 181 entities with multiple defined appearance states. Every story contains all nine memory stresses, but counts are uneven: state-change tags occur in 241 segments and persistent states in 774. Tags can overlap; these are authored opportunities, not observed generation outcomes or the scorers entity-level denominators. Story titles span settings such as lighthouse, night market, greenhouse, and subway, but no genre labels or distribution match13 C. Systems, Controls, and Reproduction C.1. Comparison Scope and Neighboring Work Relationship to neighboring memory systems. Table 12 compares the reported designs and measurements of OneStory, StoryMem, and SubjectAnchor with our study. They develop trained memory-conditioned generators and evaluate narrative quality, alignment, or identity. SubjectAnchor also explicitly studies shot-level inclusion/exclusion, so entity exclusion itself is not our novelty. Our diagnostic emphasis is the validity of selected historical evidence for the current state, its interaction with prompt information, and the distinction between reference quality and whole-policy outcomes. The table is comparison of scope, not common-protocol performance ranking; our policy effects do not establish the behavior of all three trained architectures. SubjectAnchor comparison feasibility. SubjectAnchor uses subject-aware trained architecture, 50-story benchmark, and precomputed subject-centric keyframes with Wan2.2-I2V [17]. Our shared-generator comparison uses FLUX.2 keyframe composition followed by Wan2.2-TI2V. The public preprint links no implementation or checkpoint for running its model under our protocol, so matched empirical comparison is not currently reproducible. We compare its stated task and findings, without claiming that our observed trade-off applies to every memory architecture. C.2. Causal Adapter Contract Released causal systems are driven through authors released memory mechanisms and weights with only protocolrequired substitutions; the four retrieval memories are ours and form the controlled testbed. All scored rows share frozen gold, causal guard, materialization, and scoring. No gold crop or gold identity is exposed to an ordinary system; only the privileged last-seen control uses gold IDs for reference selection (App. C.4). On Track-A, self-generated observation is replaced by the revealed real segment; if native write requires model forward, we use one teacher-forced clean-context forward without denoising. Recalled items are mapped back to source frames through temporal identities and dropped if they violate the causal guard. Methods that require future story information or modalities absent from passive film are not assigned surrogate quantitative scores. Table 13 summarizes why the families internal diagnostics are not comparable and which common observables VMemBench uses. Table 14 lists, for each memory we cite or test, what it stores, how it decides what to read, and whether and how it forgets. Figure 9. Anatomy of Track-A film (Spring, Blender Studio, CC BY 4.0). The Four Retrieval Memories Track-A retrieval definitions. The adapter stores observed segment text and sampled video frames with temporal identities. Text-frame ranks historical frames by cross-modal similarity. Seg+uniform ranks segments by text similarity and uniformly samples frames. Seg+DINO-key uses the same segment ranking, 2-fps dense sampling, and greedy farthest-point DINOv3 diversity. Seg+frame reranking performs text coarse retrieval followed by frame-level cross-modal reranking with reciprocal rank fusion. TrackA reports their native cap B=16 and the budget sweep in Fig. 5. Audited Track-B generation loop. All six sharedgenerator conditions (the four retrieval memories and the two controls) come from one run of the released testbed (vmem_bench.testbed, seed 2026): one rollout per story and condition, all generated with the same code revision and scored by the same judge. Each story starts with an empty retrieval store and an empty entity bank. At segment n, the authored prompt gn is used directly as the retrieval query. The history record for each prior segment stores that same authored prompt as both prompt text and description, together with frames decoded from that memorys own previously generated MP4; no real-film frame, gold crop, or other memorys trajectory enters the archive. Retrieval happens before write-back, with eligibility requiring the historical segment end time to be no later than the store clock. The resulting still images are then passed as composed references to shared keyframe-first stack: FLUX.2 Klein 9B-KV FP8 composes either text-only or multi-reference keyframe, and Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Turbo expands it to 121-frame segment (1280704 render, delivered at 832480). The generated segment is then appended to that memorys own store and becomes available to later segments. The retrieval reference budget is K=3; the audited code defaults are 1-fps uniform sampling, 2-fps dense sampling, top-5 text-ranked segments, three DINO keyframes per segment, and reciprocal-rank fusion with k=60 for Seg+frame reranking. The scorer is the same pinned Qwen3-VL-32B judge used for every Track-B row, applied to the frozen story gold. 15 Table 13. Different internal memories, one common interface. The families expose different internal states and native diagnostics, so those quantities are not directly comparable and do not by themselves establish what reaches or survives generation. VMem-Bench maps them to common observables: boundary context (cid:98)Cn before synthesis (Track-A) and generated outcome xn after synthesis (Track-B). Memory family Internal interface / native diagnostic What internal-only evaluation cannot establish Window / KV frames, latents, or KV; recency / native attention; cache reach Retrieval indexed frames / clips; search + rank; Recall@K / similarity Entity / state memory persistent identity / state records; address, update, filter; record validity Retention does not imply that intent-relevant evidence crosses the finite conditioning boundary; stale history may remain active. Larger can buy recall while increasing context spend or contamination; good retrieval decision may still fail in synthesis. Correct records do not guarantee that the right visual evidence is materialized under budget or realized correctly by the generator. Realization-layer scope. The reported retrieval rollouts are keyframe-first: selected stills are composed into single FLUX scene keyframe, and Wan receives that image as its first-frame condition. This is useful for holding simple realization mechanism fixed, but it introduces structural bias: memory that should emerge only later in the segment may be pulled into the first frame. The codebase also contains Wan2.2-I2V-A14B backends with SVI/Morphic LoRA variants, but the reported Track-B retrieval rows did not use those paths; they used Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Turbo. unified multimodal reference-conditioned generator such as MiniMax H3 [12], which accepts text, image, video, and audio context directly, is natural future replacement because it may avoid collapsing multiple memory cues into one forced first-frame keyframe. When we designed the Track-B realization setup, H3 had not yet been open-sourced; the main results therefore use the FLUX-to-Wan scaffold. We have since run all six conditions on 8 stories with two H3 realizations (App. F.6, Table 22); we make no claim that H3 improves VMem-Bench scores. Provenance. The testbeds production files are internally 0indexed whereas Track-B gold is 1-indexed, so scoring reads view that maps GT seg_k to production seg_{k-1}. Every condition scores all 2,824/2,824 segments. The release pins the code revision and the scored snapshots rather than moving source tree. 16 C.4. Last-Seen Reference Control For Track-B segment n, the control reads the gold cast and keeps the characters and props that must appear and have appeared before. It orders them by gap (longest first), keeps up to three, and for each takes the middle frame of this rollouts own clip of the segment in which the entity last appeared; duplicates are merged. The generator receives only these frames, never gold text, names, or images, and guard admits only clips that this run produced strictly before segment n. Because the needed entity was usually on screen just before, 1,803 segments receive one reference, 842 two, 149 three, and 30 (the first segment of each story) none. The control shows what memory gains by choosing the right entity at its latest moment; it is not an information upper bound, since it hands over fewer references than retrieval and its frame may itself be wrong earlier rendering. C.5. Released Causal-Memory Systems LongLive-RAG. Each revealed Track-A segment is VAE-encoded to Wan latents [16] with the released LongLive-RAG [4] wrapper and published LatentAE. The released latent-memory rule performs cosine top-k retrieval with memory_size=6, recent_exclude=5, and sink_size=1. Track-B uses the released generatorcoupled system. MemFlow. MemFlow [7] combines recent window with compressed long-term KV bank. We teacher-force each revealed Track-A segment through the released base+LoRA clean-context commit path, record the local window and surviving bank blocks, and recover source frames via bitexact fingerprints of retained KV blocks. The temporal RoPE table is extended to the film length with the same closed-form rotary embedding. Track-B uses the released generator-coupled path. IAMFlow. IAMFlow [8] scores frames using the native diffusion transformers KV cache. Its offline driver precomputes entities from the full prompt list; our causal adapter disables this future look-ahead and uses native per-prompt processing. Track-B uses the released generator-coupled stack. Track-A is reported only as scalability diagnostic because the native per-frame KV archive exceeds host memory on long films. C.6. IAMFlow Track-A Scalability IAMFlows native long-term archive copies per-frame K/V slices to host memory. For its Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B backbone, one archived frame costs approximately 30 2 1560 1536 2 bytes 274 MiB. Redundancy then uses multimembership groups, so reference that covers several gold entities contributes to each of those groups rather than to an arbitrary first label. RV is repeated-view redundancy inside those groups, and RS is the pair-weighted mean DINOv3 cosine among crops of the same entity. Headline Precision, Recall, and F1 are not rewritten by that grouping. Dataset numbers are unweighted means over films segments, then over films. Causal guard and budget sweeps. Every reference carries source time and is materialized at that recalled time. Any item at or after the current segment start is dropped. Identity Measurement and Calibration The presence judge checks each entity against its gold description only, so it cannot tell returning character from description-matching stranger. Two versioned scorers in VMem-Bench measure identity directly; the full protocol, prompts, thresholds, and model installer are in the benchmarks scoring documentation. Units. From the frozen gold, one unit per return of character or prop that was absent in the previous segment but seen before (1,130 units), plus seeded 20% sample of returns from the previous segment (583) and the characters that return changed after 30 or more segments (61). The previous appearance is the latest earlier segment whose cast lists the entity; both appearances come from the same rollout of the same condition. VLM pairwise judge (trackB-identity-1.0). The judge receives both strips, the entitys name, kind, and gold description at each appearance (with note when state change is expected), is told to ignore camera, pose, lighting, and background, and answers in JSON whether the entity is visible in each strip and, if in both, whether it is the same individual (face, hair, build, clothing; shape, color, material, markings for props). Discussion, Limitations, and Future Tests H.1. What the Closed-Loop Comparison Identifies Each policy writes its own history, so Track-B compares complete policies. Reference-count strata are also unmatched. To isolate references effect, branch from the same story prefix and generator state, fix the prompt, seed, and reference count, then replace one reference with current-state, stale-state, or distractor-filtered alternative. Score required appearances, requested-state fidelity, and forbidden entities separately, so any reduction in interference is read alongside lost useful context. Use the instruction-valid state, including an older state for an explicit flashback. These interventions remain future work; pairing seeds alone would not identify single-reference effect once histories diverge. H.2. Design Hypotheses and Falsification The 224-unit single-author audit uses an earlier sharedgenerator rollout. Among sampled, judge-flagged requiredentity misses, inclusion-weighted shares are 29% writing, 36% selection, 7% synthesis, and 27% judge misses (App. G). These conditional shares are not population failure frequencies. They motivate tests of necessity (information absent from prompt and recent context), temporal validity (the state requested now, including deliberate flashbacks), and non-interference (unrequested content in useful frames). Failure attribution uses one authors stratified inspection of an earlier rollout and does not yield population-level causal partition of all failure modes. External validity. Track-B uses 30 authored, entitylabeled stories and shared keyframe-plus-video pipeline; the alternative video-backend check covers eight stories. Track-A uses two real-film datasets but does not test downstream generation on those exact segments. Our title asks whether providing historical memory helps; we have not established how performance varies monotonically with storage capacity, reference count, or every type of state-aware memory architecture. The results should not be generalized to all genres, interactive policies, or models without further evidence. Scope of design implications. Table 25 proposes tests, not established remedies. Prompt stripping does not validate reading gate, and whole-rollout avoidance losses do not validate content filtering. Each proposal requires its own matched intervention and can fail while the measurement distinctions remain useful. Broader generators, seed variation, and interactive stories remain outside the demonstrated scope.
